title: Five AI-Assisted Films Win India's Google Flow Filmathon and Head to IFFI Goa
excerpt:
Five filmmakers from across India have won the inaugural WIF India x Google Flow Filmathon.
Their AI-assisted shorts will screen at the International Film Festival of India in Goa.
body_md:
Five films created with Google's AI filmmaking workspace Flow have been selected as winners of the inaugural WIF India x Google Flow Filmathon. The projects are scheduled to screen on Monday, November 23, 2026, at the International Film Festival of India in Goa. Their makers represent a broad geographic spread, from Kerala to the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, underscoring the organizers' ambition to reach storytellers beyond India's established production centers.

Women in Film India partnered with Google Flow to offer emerging filmmakers an opportunity to experiment with AI-assisted storytelling. The open call attracted more than 850 registrations, with 60 percent coming from Tier 1 cities, 30 percent from Tier 2 cities and 10 percent from Tier 3 cities. Women directed three of the five winning films, a result the organizers highlighted as an encouraging sign for participation in an evolving filmmaking landscape.

Two winners are based in Kerala. Calicut filmmaker Aswathi Naduthodi made Bombay Mumbai – Vada Pav, a visual essay tracing decades of change in Mumbai through the people connected to its iconic street food. Kochi-based Syam Manohar directed Kuli, a Tamil-language black comedy in which a stranger digging a peculiar hole unleashes an escalating chain of village gossip. The films demonstrate different uses of AI-assisted production: one examines a changing city, while the other builds a fictional situation around community behavior.

From Port Blair in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Promita Banerjee contributed Sikkal, a Hindi folk-horror story about grief and guilt. Its protagonist is haunted by apparitions of his deceased sister. Mumbai filmmaker Nikhil Shinde's Pedals of Joy is a Hindi animated tale about brotherhood centered on a young balloon seller who dreams of owning a sports bike. Delhi-based Srishti Chaudhary made Nazar, a dialogue-free animation using visual metaphors to explore the burden of an unwanted gaze. Chaudhary developed the project's character sheets and storyboards inside Google Flow.

A seven-person jury selected the winners. Its members included directors Shakun Batra and Pan Nalin, editor Nitin Baid, editor-director Deepa Bhatia, film and streaming executive Aparna Purohit, Google's Prashant Paulose, and Sten Saluveer, who leads Cannes Next at the Cannes Film Market. The range of expertise involved places the selected projects in a wider filmmaking conversation rather than presenting them simply as demonstrations of a technology platform.

WIF India founder and CEO Guneet Monga Kapoor framed the initiative around a question that accompanies major technological changes: who gains the ability to make films, whose perspectives are represented, and who helps shape the medium's future? She particularly welcomed the fact that three selected projects came from women. Programs and development director Rabia Chopra also emphasized that expensive equipment, professional connections and formal training have historically created barriers for emerging storytellers.

The Entertainment Society of Goa and the Government of Goa are supporting the IFFI presentation, giving the filmmakers an opportunity to show their work to an industry audience. The announcement confirms competition wins and a festival screening, not general theatrical distribution or streaming deals. The larger significance lies in testing whether more accessible production tools can expand participation while keeping human storytelling choices at the heart of each film.
seo_title: Five AI Films Win Google Flow Filmathon at IFFI Goa
seo_description: Five AI-assisted films from across India win the WIF India x Google Flow Filmathon and secure an IFFI Goa screening, including three works by women.
